claims.text: Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies, in which businesses source, produce and sell across national borders and goods, services, money and people move between countries more freely than before.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Globalisation has grown mainly because transport and communication have become far cheaper, because governments have reduced the barriers that once protected national markets, and because multinational businesses expanding across borders have pulled their suppliers and customers into worldwide networks.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Globalisation is not the same as selling abroad: exporting is one activity a single business chooses, whereas globalisation is an economy-wide process that changes how whole industries source, produce and sell.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An opportunity of globalisation is a chance the growing world market gives a business to improve its position, such as selling to customers in new countries or buying inputs from a wider range of suppliers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Globalisation can threaten a business because it brings larger foreign competitors into its home market and can make the business dependent on foreign suppliers or foreign demand, conditions it does not control.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The main opportunities globalisation offers a business are a larger potential market, cheaper or better sources of supply, and access to ideas and technology from around the world; the main threats are foreign competitors entering the home market and dependence on suppliers and customers abroad.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An import tariff is a tax a government places on goods entering the country; an import quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that may be brought in over a period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Governments typically introduce import tariffs or quotas to protect home producers and the jobs that depend on them from foreign competition, and a tariff can also raise revenue for the government.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A tariff or quota tends to raise the price of imported goods in the home market, which shifts some sales towards home producers but leaves consumers paying more and can invite other countries to tax this country's exports in reply.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Tariffs and quotas are trade restrictions that act at the border on what may enter a country, whereas legal controls such as pollution rules or safety standards regulate how businesses operate inside the economy.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A multinational business is a business with its headquarters in one country, its home country, and operations it controls in at least one other country, its host countries.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business may become a multinational to produce closer to foreign customers, to buy materials or labour more cheaply, to avoid trade barriers by producing inside a market, and to spread its risks across several countries.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Becoming a multinational changes the position of the business's stakeholders in different directions: owners gain the chance of higher profits but carry more risk, home-country workers may see roles move to the new location, host-country workers gain jobs, and suppliers and governments in each country are affected differently.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Shareholders are the owners of a company and are one stakeholder group, whereas stakeholders are all the groups affected by the business's decisions, including workers, customers, suppliers, lenders and governments.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A country where a multinational locates can gain jobs at the plant and among local suppliers, exports when the plant sells abroad, wider consumer choice, and investment in buildings, equipment and training.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Investment by a multinational is the money it spends in the host country on buildings, machinery, infrastructure and training, creating productive capacity and jobs there rather than in its home country.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Local businesses in a host country can lose sales when a multinational arrives, because it may produce at lower cost and carry a brand customers already know, which can force local firms to cut output or close.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Repatriation of profits is the sending of a multinational's profits back to its home country rather than keeping or reinvesting them in the host country where they were earned.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Whether a host country gains or loses from a multinational depends on conditions such as how much of the plant's spending goes to local suppliers, whether profits are reinvested there, and whether local businesses can withstand the new competition.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An exchange rate is the price of one country's currency expressed in another country's currency.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Appreciation means one unit of a country's currency buys more foreign currency than before, and depreciation means one unit buys less; they are the two opposite directions in which the same rate can move.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The boundary between appreciation and depreciation is the direction of what one unit of the home currency buys abroad: more foreign currency is appreciation, whereas less is depreciation, and the same movement seen from the foreign currency's side runs the opposite way.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: When a currency depreciates, each unit of it buys less foreign currency, so goods priced in that foreign currency become dearer for home buyers and home-produced goods become cheaper for foreign buyers; appreciation reverses both effects.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Competitiveness is a business's ability to win sales against rival products, which depends on the price it must charge and on everything else customers value, such as quality, reliability and brand.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A depreciation tends to hurt a business that imports materials, because they cost more in the home currency and squeeze its margins unless it can pass the cost on, while the same movement tends to help an exporter, because its prices fall for foreign buyers; an appreciation reverses the pattern, helping importers and squeezing exporters.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business that imports materials and also exports products meets both effects at once, and which one dominates depends on which side of its trading is larger and on how it responds, for example by sourcing more materials at home.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Globalisation and multinational businesses are not the same: a multinational is one kind of business, with operations it controls in more than one country, whereas globalisation is an economy-wide process whose opportunities and threats can reach businesses that operate in one country, such as a local firm facing imported competition or buying imported inputs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
